analysis.one_liner: Rewrites pesticide residue rules around a single health-based standard, adds explicit protections for infants and children, and blocks states from setting stricter pesticide limits.
analysis.headline: The Senate Agriculture Committee approved this bipartisan pesticide-safety rewrite in July 1996, but the full Senate never voted on it; Congress instead passed a near-identical Food Quality Protection Act that August.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the old, fragmented rules for pesticide residues in food with one health-based standard, require the EPA to re-evaluate existing tolerances with the health of infants and children in mind, and spend more on testing food for residues. It would also legalize small, 'negligible' dietary risks from cancer-causing pesticides that current law bans outright, extend pesticide makers' exclusive rights to their safety data, and stop states from enforcing pesticide limits stricter than the federal ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Food consumers get a uniform, health-based residue standard explicitly designed to protect infants and children, plus more monitoring of imported and domestic food. Specialty-crop growers get minor-use programs, expedited registrations, and federal matching funds to keep crop-protection tools available for small-acreage crops. Pesticide manufacturers gain a predictable national standard, the end of the zero-carcinogen rule for processed foods, longer exclusive data rights, and freedom from stricter state rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, specialty growers, pesticide makers

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA, USDA, and HHS to set procedures ensuring pesticide tolerances safeguard infants and children, carrying out the National Research Council's report 'Pesticides in the Diets of Infants and Children,' and requires toxicity testing and risk assessment methods that account for children's vulnerability.

Requires the EPA to reassess every pesticide tolerance as part of reregistration and replaces the old patchwork (including the zero-risk Delaney rule for processed foods) with a single 'negligible dietary risk' standard that the Administrator must be able to defend on public-health grounds.

Extends the tolerance framework to processed food, deeming it not adulterated when residues fall within the raw-commodity tolerance, and authorizes an additional $12 million for monitoring pesticide residues in imported and domestic food.

Creates EPA and USDA minor-use programs, expedited review of minor-use registrations, and a $10 million-per-year matching fund program to keep crop-protection chemicals available for small-acreage crops that large registrants have little incentive to serve.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new monitoring and matching-fund programs (authorized at $12 million and $10 million per year). State governments lose the power to set or enforce pesticide residue limits — including warning-label requirements — that differ from federal tolerances, unless they win a hard EPA petition process. Pesticide registrants pay new fees for tolerance petitions and bear the cost of mandatory tolerance re-evaluations.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars states and localities from establishing or enforcing any residue limit — including warning requirements — on qualifying pesticides that differs from the federal tolerance, except through an EPA petition showing 'compelling local conditions,' and bars states from acting on residues that were lawful at the time of application unless they show an unreasonable dietary risk.

It replaces the Delaney clause's zero-tolerance standard for carcinogens in processed food with a 'negligible dietary risk' standard, so some pesticide residues that current law prohibits outright would become legal at low levels.

It extends pesticide registrants' exclusive control over their safety data from 10 to as long as 13 years, lets the EPA waive data requirements for minor uses, and exempts minor-use registration reviews from judicial review — reducing the data and oversight available for safety decisions in exchange for faster, cheaper registrations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The child-health provisions are the bill's real strength: a uniform standard built around infants' and children's exposure, mandatory tolerance re-evaluations, and more residue monitoring address a documented gap that the National Academy of Sciences had flagged. The honest costs are real but narrower: the negligible-risk standard abandons an absolute (and widely considered outdated) zero-cancer rule, the preemption clause strips states of a tool they had used to go further than EPA, and the minor-use exclusivity and data waivers tilt the playing field toward registrants. On balance it is a genuine compromise package, not a giveaway — which is why its near-copy attracted broad bipartisan support.

outcome.mechanism: The Agriculture Committee held hearings, folded in two companion bills, and approved the bill favorably in July 1996, but the Senate never brought it to a floor vote before the Congress ended — and a near-identical Food Quality Protection Act was enacted later that year through the House.

narrative.text: Introduced August 10, 1995 by Senator Lugar with nine original cosponsors from both parties, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The committee held hearings on June 12, 1996.
On July 24, 1996 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, incorporating provisions of related measures S. 794 and S. 1491.
No further Senate action followed before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill never received a Senate floor vote.

In August 1996, Congress enacted the Food Quality Protection Act of 1996 (P.L. 104-170), a closely related rewrite of pesticide law that included the health-based tolerance standard, children's-health protections, and national uniformity of tolerances, so the substance of S. 1166 largely became law through another vehicle.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because a near-identical law passed the same year, neither side was left with much to show for the bill's death: pesticide makers and food processors won national preemption of stricter state rules in the enacted law, while children's-health advocates won the uniform health-based standard. The main thing lost was a Senate vote on the compromise itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Both sides — a near-identical law passed anyway

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 34 cosponsors split 23 Republicans and 11 Democrats, with original cosponsors including Dole (R-KS), Pryor (D-AR), Inouye (D-HI), Kerrey (D-NE), and Breaux (D-LA) — and the record shows no organized opposition; the bill simply never reached a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill gives registrants a predictable national standard, ends the zero-carcinogen Delaney rule for processed food, extends exclusive data rights up to 13 years, waives some data requirements, and preempts stricter state limits. In exchange it imposes mandatory tolerance re-evaluations, a larger science review board, coordination of cancellations with tolerance revocations, and fees.

Minor-use programs, expedited one-year reviews, data waivers, and a $10 million matching fund program keep crop-protection tools available for small-acreage crops the market under-serves, which also supports the supply and price of fruits and vegetables for consumers.

By extending the tolerance framework to processed food and deeming it not adulterated when residues fall within the raw-commodity tolerance, the bill resolves a legal conflict under the old Delaney rule that made processed food vulnerable to being treated as adulterated.

National uniformity bars states from enforcing any residue limit — including warning-label rules — that differs from federal tolerances for qualifying pesticides, unless they win an EPA petition showing compelling local conditions. What states lose here runs alongside what consumers lose: the option of stricter local protection.
